title: I Let the Essential-Oil Distiller Clock Catch the Chair Who Left My Numbered Flask

parts.text: I stepped into the still bench at 11:08 a.m. and chair Rowan was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE STILL. TWO HOURS. FLASKS STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was thirty-two, studio secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered flask. Rowan shrugged. "Chairs are the still." I photographed the board, the booking, and his leftover hydrosol on my numbered flask. Then I asked for the still log. At 11:16 the desk pinged why Rowan's name was on my hydrosol. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The desk can see Rowan's leftover hydrosol on my numbered flask.

social.video_title: He left my numbered distiller flask on my still — Part 1/2
social.description: Still bench, leftover hydrosol, a two-hour clock he posted. I logged the flask. Would you have asked for the still log?

parts.text: Rowan called it cohobation until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the hydrosol still. The flask went back to my numbered slot. Rowan ran a slot of his own and told the next chair atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CHAIRS ARE NOT THE STILL. I keep my flask on a labeled shelf. Rowan brown-bags his cohobation. The bench finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Still log, numbered flask, and a second line on the board. Was cohobation ever my hydrosol?
